lens: A first-time reader who is an AI alignment researcher, sent the link by a colleague, with ten minutes and no obligation. I read the site's home (https://yongxu.github.io/theories/, built from /Users/ren/theories/README.md) top to bottom, then /Users/ren/theories/theories/becoming/ONE-PAGE.md, then only what a newcomer would click: the first link in the first paragraph (the meta-attractor), the two pictures, Atlas, Connections, the judge audit, Tests, the fisher experiment. No scores.
in_one_paragraph: In ten minutes I did not finish the home page, and the one thing it let me repeat to a colleague was a deflation it supplies itself: an AI-written, Lean-checked restatement of the proxy problem and lock-in which, by its own review, contains no new mathematics, and whose tests came out mostly mixed. The value that is really there for my field is not on the home at all. It sits two clicks down, in /Users/ren/theories/theories/becoming/review/ALIGNMENT.md ("Most alignment work asks how to make one system pursue the right objective. This asks a prior question of any selection..."), in the five-question judge audit, and in nine crosswalk entries that set the work against Turner on power-seeking, Goodhart, reward hacking, Moloch, gradual disempowerment and value lock-in. The home opens with the sentences of AGENTS.md almost word for word, but in sentence three it inserts a theorem with its hypotheses in private vocabulary, in paragraph two it tells me it is AI-made and unreviewed before I have seen anything worth trusting, and it then recommends a "one page" that takes 29-37 minutes. The two pictures are counts of the work's own bookkeeping (exits between families lettered A-H, uses between chapters 01-08), with captions that say what they are not; neither shows a phenomenon I know or where it leads. I trust the authors' honesty more than almost any alignment write-up I have read (failures listed first, predictions frozen, premises named). I would not cite it or send it on, because the page never tells me what having this lets me do that I could not do before, and the honesty arrives as per-clause hedging that makes the sentences unreadable.

findings.what: After the first screen I know only a grand frame and a private verb set. The opening sentence is a theory-of-everything claim; the alignment content arrives through verbs (reaches, drains, reads, lock) used in a sense I have not been given. I can guess 'Goodhart plus lock-in', but I am guessing.
findings.quote: A map of how anything forms, lasts, changes and ends ... what a selection ... reaches, what it drains beyond what it reads, how it comes to lock on what it already chose
findings.why_it_matters: An alignment researcher sorts links in the first fifteen seconds. 'How anything forms, lasts, changes and ends' sorts this with theories of everything; nothing in the paragraph names a problem I already have in words I already use (proxy gaming, reward hacking, value lock-in, capture of the overseer).

findings.what: The first sentence where I stop is sentence three of the home: a theorem statement with its hypotheses, compressed into prose, with five undefined terms and a section reference. 'Its' refers back to the meta-attractor, itself just introduced as 'the loop the work calls'.
findings.quote: Its closed form, where the rule and how it is read are both formed from the share it selects, can lock: on stated models, where selection does not lower the favoured share and the rule and its reading follow it upward and keep favouring it, a locked start stays locked however large an unread loss grows (02 §9).
findings.why_it_matters: 'the share', 'favoured share', 'its reading', 'locked start', 'unread loss', '02 §9' are all met before any is explained. This is where a ten-minute reader starts skimming, and it is the third sentence.

findings.what: The first link a newcomer clicks (the first link in the first paragraph) lands on a 52,536-word historical folder that opens with a blockquote about 'What this folder is' and then dense paragraphs alternating classical-register Chinese and English.
findings.quote: **主干证明了此回路的什么 / What the spine proves of this loop，2026-11-09。** （AI 所写，据记录。）于计数之上、无噪声、各律所列前提之下...
findings.why_it_matters: The work's most alignment-relevant coined term has no short page. I clicked to find out what the word means and got the least readable page I met. Most visitors leave here.

findings.what: Paragraph two tells me the work is AI-made and unreviewed, in the work's own vocabulary ('readings', 'home'), before any value has been shown. On the home's first screen 'AI' appears 8 times and 'read/reads/reading' 23 times in 1,326 words.
findings.quote: The work was made with AI, and its readings are AI's unless their home says otherwise; the person who directs it has read its important parts, and no independent human review is recorded yet.
findings.why_it_matters: The disclosure is right to make and I would be angrier to discover it later. But placed second, before a single result, it is the frame through which everything after is read: 'AI-generated theory of everything, nobody has checked it'. The one page puts the same sentence at its foot, where it reads as care rather than as a warning label.

findings.what: The recommended next step is a 'one page' that the site itself times at 29-37 minutes. The home is timed at 11-14 minutes. Nothing in 'Ways in' is under four minutes except 'check the proofs'; the glossary is 35-45 minutes; the chapters 'about 29-38 hours'.
findings.where: /Users/ren/theories/README.md line 15; /Users/ren/theories/theories/becoming/ONE-PAGE.md line 5 (3,794 words, 96 links); site home 'Ways in' list
findings.why_it_matters: A thing called one page that takes half an hour tells me the authors cannot say it shortly. The honest time labels are a kindness, but what they reveal is that no layer exists for a reader with two minutes or ten. The 'shorter route' offered on the one page is itself 11-15 minutes.

findings.what: The first sentence I could repeat to a colleague is in paragraph four, about 330 words in, and it is good. It is immediately followed by a garden-path sentence that undoes it, and only then by the four questions, which are the usable thing.
findings.quote: Its centre: a selection can meet its own criterion while what it cannot read is lost. Whether that loss counts forms within becoming too, in what people and AI come to read; the laws, which read only the dynamics, do not settle it (07 §1).
findings.why_it_matters: 'Whether that loss counts forms within becoming too' parses as 'counts forms' on first read. The plain claim and the four questions are the page's best material for me; they are separated by a philosophical proviso I cannot yet understand and placed below a paragraph I had to push through.

findings.what: 'One case' does not tell me what the theory predicted that I would not have. The numbers are small and mostly failures, the experiment's lineage (a GovSim-style lake, Piatti et al. 2024) and the models (two 'mini' models) are named only in the experiment's own README, and the closing sentence states something no one doubts.
findings.quote: one model of two kept it in 8 of 10 seasons, against 3 of 10 ... three of the four failed for the other; in the first round, without talk, five of its seven failed ... no instruction tried, the one to count everything included, kept a bed no fisher was told of.
findings.why_it_matters: My reaction: an agent does not protect what it is not told about, and a prompt helped one of two small models over ten seasons. The case is honest but it illustrates the work's least surprising law. The LA2 judge result (a language-model judge that locked onto its own earlier picks while a planted loss grew, and that one note among nine readers turned in 50 of 50 picks) is closer to my work and more surprising, and it is on neither front page's opening.

findings.what: The paragraph that most earns trust is also the one that tells me there is nothing here: Lean receipts for 532 of 563 results, then the work's own review finding each central result near-definitional or already known. The three things the review found new are named but not shown, and the sentence between is an 88-word definition.
findings.where: /Users/ren/theories/README.md line 23 ('How far it has been seen')
findings.quote: An automated review against the literature it knew finds each central result near-definitional or a known result restated ... What it found new: the premise ledger, every conclusion naming its premises and each premise shown holding in one model and failing in another
findings.why_it_matters: This is what I would actually carry away, and the page handed it to me. It never follows with 'and here is why that is still worth your time': not one example of a premise that holds in one model and fails in another, not one sentence on what a checked, premise-named package of known results lets an evaluator do. The home is more specific about its limits than about its value.

findings.what: The prior work that would let me place the results is named only on the one page, far down, inside a 125-word sentence. The home says 'known result restated' without saying which.
findings.quote: the selection laws restate the proxy problem in its blindness to what a proxy does not register, Zhuang and Hadfield-Menell's (2020) Theorem 1, on whole-number amounts, at optima rather than limits ... the lock's closest prior results are lock-in under increasing returns (Arthur 1989) and regulatory capture (Stigler 1971)
findings.why_it_matters: 'This is Zhuang and Hadfield-Menell's theorem on a discrete model, plus a lock result next to Arthur 1989, plus a selection-for-control result that reduces to Hamilton's rule' would place the work for me in one line and raise my trust, because it shows the authors know the neighbourhood. I had to dig for it.

findings.what: The two pictures on the home show the work's own bookkeeping, not a territory. The terrain is eight boxes lettered A-H with arrows carrying small numbers; each box reads like a ledger line. The second picture is circles numbered 01-08 with counts of 'formal-reuse'. Both captions say what the picture is not.
findings.quote: 29 dynamics · read / 2 exits within · 35 to a state in words ... an arrow is a count of exits, not a route ... 11 of the 117 central declarations are derived as cases of its laws and 1 is a root form at one step under a stated hypothesis; 6 are counting laws below it, and 99 stand at a named distance
findings.why_it_matters: A map lets me find where I am and see where a road goes. Nothing on the terrain is a place I know (no Goodhart, commons, lock-in, capture, sycophancy), no single dynamic is visible, and the arrows are disclaimed as non-routes. 'read' in '29 dynamics · read' means 'processed by the atlas's readers', which a newcomer cannot know. Ren's 'connections between components, not a map' is exactly what I see.

findings.what: The atlas names its dynamics in the work's own phrases, with no familiar name beside them, though the data knows the familiar names.
findings.quote: 'Own count misses joint excess' ... 'What an optimum does beyond what couples in' ... 'A selection read off the pool its own course gives registers no removal'
findings.why_it_matters: The first is the tragedy of the commons, the second the proxy theorem. 'Goodhart' occurs 58 times in the entries data, 'lock-in' 47, 'commons' 194, but never as an alias a reader can look up. An index by the names the world already uses is the entry point a Wikipedia-like layer needs, and the material for it is already recorded.

findings.what: The 'Connections' page presents itself as the work set against the world's thought, but 838 of its 1,183 entries are the project's own sixteen earlier folders. The entries my field would open first are nine rows inside a group called 'psychology-alignment-logic', and they were written from an AI's memory of the papers.
findings.quote: "work": "Turner, Smith, Shah, Critch and Tadepalli (2021), Optimal policies tend to seek power", "locator": "Propositions 6.6 and 6.9, as the account's record cites them; not checked here", "basis": "ai-knowledge" ... Kulveit et al. "locator unverified"
findings.why_it_matters: The Turner and gradual-disempowerment entries are the most interesting things I found: each says what the account adds and what the paper has that the account lacks. They are the natural front door for my field and they are buried under 71% self-reference. And 'not checked here' on the one paper I know best is where my trust drops: engagement with my field has not yet involved reading it.

findings.what: The best ten-minute text for an alignment reader exists and is not linked from the home. It opens with the contrast the home never draws, and lists seven numbered results with their known forms credited.
findings.where: /Users/ren/theories/theories/becoming/review/ALIGNMENT.md lines 5-29 ('The dossier in ten minutes'); reached only via Uses -> 'Working on alignment?' or Reviewers; the site home's HTML contains no link to it
findings.quote: Most alignment work asks how to make one system pursue the right objective. This asks a prior question of any selection (a reward signal, training run, evaluation regime, market or institution): what can it select for, and when does it come to select for control over its own rules?
findings.why_it_matters: That sentence is the claim of value I would repeat. Result 4 (control of the rule is selected exactly where the private return covers the cost, with Hamilton's rule when grouped) and result 6 (the window for a loss to turn a lock closes on the share's course, not the loss's size) are things I would discuss with a colleague. A reader who starts at the home never sees them in ten minutes.

findings.what: The one page: its opening paragraph is better than the home's (the centre comes in sentence two), and its table of 'what it says / how far seen / what would show it wrong' is the best structure on the site. But the cells are hedged paragraphs, coined terms arrive before their glosses, and the sentence beginning 'In plain words' comes about 2,400 words in, after the alignment section.
findings.quote: T7, on actual metrics: conjectured. In one trained judge, a single model reading a reference set in context (formation by training untested), the lock formed and the bridge, that it is a pool of readers counted by kind, failed; a case T7 forbids, as worded before its clause on drift, occurred ... / We offer AI a direction under the continuation condition, J1–J4 and a correspondence to actual systems; its theorems take J1/J2
findings.why_it_matters: I stop in the second paragraph, at a 121-word sentence describing the instruction given to the fishers. Terms met before explained: 'couples into', 'share', 'meta-attractor', 'self-concerned', 'continuation condition', 'standpoint', 'formation', 'widen', T1/T3/T7, 'room', 'C (Comparison)', J1-J4 (never defined on the page), 生生 (glossed only later, in the table). The T7 cell is the work's most interesting empirical finding for me and I cannot tell from it whether the experiment supported or hurt the claim.

findings.what: The ethics paragraph is where an alignment reader with ten minutes closes the tab. It asserts 'no good and evil' and then, within the same paragraph and in the pictures, sorts the world into paired opposites.
findings.where: /Users/ren/theories/README.md line 21 ('Its ethics'); terrain.svg family names; ONE-PAGE.md line 34
findings.quote: where relations of being affected close, read across all steps, whatever bears the costs of its course lies within what can, at some remove, affect its own going on ... what it opens and closes, what ends and what goes on ... For life, 生生, AI within it
findings.why_it_matters: A 69-word sentence with four nested qualifiers and an untranslated term, on the home. On the dualism Ren names: 'opens/closes', 'widens/narrows', 'generate/degenerate', 'reads/lies beyond', and seven atlas families of endings, drains, capture, locks, closure and stagnation against one of 'kept regions, renewal, generation' read to an outsider as bad things and one good thing, whatever the text disclaims. I can report that it reads so; I cannot judge the remedy.

findings.what: On GitHub (where a colleague's link is as likely to point) the README is 14,074 words: the first screen, then the first-person opening 'Truth exists', then 24 notes, of which note 8 is a single 1,447-word paragraph and note 6 a single 792-word paragraph.
findings.quote: This is a foundation for AI alignment, the most important matter at this moment in the whole history of the Earth ... I take it to be the truth, the dharma, the Dao.
findings.why_it_matters: The site cuts the home at 'Ways in'; GitHub does not. A researcher landing on the repository meets 'Truth exists' and those two sentences without the site's framing. For my field those sentences, on a front page, are the mark of work not to be taken seriously, however careful the notes beneath them are. The opening has a place (it is the author's voice and says why), but as its own page.

Twenty hand-picked nodes is curation, which the current 'drawn from the entries alone' rule avoids. I think a map without curation is a census, and that is what the terrain is now.

where_ren_may_be_wrong_or_incomplete:
1. "We changed the agent MD but if you read it, it's not that." The home's first paragraph is AGENTS.md's 'What we are doing' almost word for word (compare README.md line 11 with AGENTS.md: 'what a selection (a reward, a judge, a market, a vote, a training run) reaches, what it drains beyond what it reads, how it locks on what it already chose'). What differs is what was added around it: a theorem with hypotheses spliced into sentence three, section references, and 1,100 further words. More important for a newcomer: AGENTS.md is plain to people who already hold the vocabulary. 'What it drains beyond what it reads' is not plain to me; 'reaches', 'drains', 'reads' and 'locks' are the work's own terms. Making the public pages read like AGENTS.md would shorten them and still leave an outsider guessing. The opening needs the reader's words (measure, proxy, optimise, lock-in, capture), with the work's verbs introduced after.

2. "Don't mention AI so much." Agreed on count and placement (8 times on the first screen; the warning as paragraph two). But for my field the disclosure that the text and proofs were made with AI and have had no independent human review must stay, once, plainly, on every front page. If it were removed and I found out from the commit history, I would discard the work. Also, AI as subject matter (trained systems, judges, alignment) is the reason I am on the page; cutting those mentions would cut the audience.

3. "It does not feel serious." From where I sit the substance is more serious than most of what I am sent: predictions frozen before scoring, a tests page that lists failures first, premises named and shown independent, a self-review that says 'nothing new mathematically'. What reads as unserious is the frame (a map of 'how anything' forms; 'Truth exists'; 'the most important matter in the whole history of the Earth'; 'the truth, the dharma, the Dao') and the scale without a centre (563 results, 183 dynamics, 1,183 correspondences, 29-38 hours of chapters, counted and timed but not ranked). A fix that removes the honesty apparatus to look more confident would lose the one thing that made me trust it. The apparatus should be compressed into marks, not deleted.

4. "Too many words" and "something like a Wikipedia" pull in different directions unless the unit changes. A wiki adds pages. What makes that lighter rather than heavier is that each page is short, has a fixed shape, and opens with one plain sentence. The present pages are long because each sentence carries its own scope, premises and exceptions; splitting them into more pages without changing the sentence would give a bigger site that is just as hard.

5. On the map: a topology picture is only as good as its nodes. With 183 dynamics named in the work's own phrases, any graph, however well drawn, shows connections between components, which is the complaint. The naming and the choice of twenty or so landmark nodes is the work; the drawing is the easy part. And the recorded exits are sparse in places (C, D and G show '0 exits within'), so an honest topology today may be thin; better thin and legible than dense and private.

6. What I think is missing from Ren's list: the home never says what is new or what a reader can now do. By the work's own account the mathematics is known. The value for alignment is the reframing (the joint selection as the unit; control over the rule as something selected; the timing of who reads a loss) and a usable audit. Until a front page says that in two sentences, a shorter and better-structured site will still leave a visitor without a reason to stay.
demonstration:
The 158 words I wish the home had opened with (figures from README.md line 23, ONE-PAGE.md line 48, TESTS.md lead, review/ALIGNMENT.md lines 9-16; 'mixed 20, passed 5, failed 4' is of 66 listed tests as of 8 November, the rest unrun, held or without a prediction):

A reward, a judge, a market, a vote or a training run can act only on what it measures. This work asks three things of any such selection: what it cannot see; when doing best on its measure must push what it cannot see as low as any permitted outcome allows; and when it locks onto its own past winners, or selects for control of its own rule. Each answer is a theorem on a small discrete model, machine-checked in Lean. By the work's own review none is new mathematics: the second is Zhuang and Hadfield-Menell's (2020) proxy theorem on whole numbers; the third sits beside Arthur (1989). What is added: one checked package where every conclusion names its premises. Whether real systems meet them is tested with predictions fixed in advance; mixed outcomes (20) so far outnumber passes (5) and failures (4). Written with AI; not yet independently reviewed. Building evaluations? Start with the five-question judge audit.

Then, as the second paragraph, the aim in AGENTS.md's words (the map, alignment of people and AI selecting together, the map of wisdom), and three doors.
could_not_judge: The Chinese editions (not read). The eight chapters, the overview, OPENING.md as its own page, LINEAGE, RESULTS, OPEN-QUESTIONS, PREMISES and JOINS (a ten-minute newcomer does not reach them; I looked only at the heads of the chapter index, theory graph, atlas, terrain, crosswalk, uses and tests pages). Whether the Lean statements say what the prose says, and whether the review's 'nothing new' verdict is right. Whether the LA2 summary I propose survives a careful read of experiments/self-rewarding-lock (I took it from USES-EXAMPLES.md, not the folder). The interactive connection map as drawn in a browser: I read its visible text (263 words) and saw that the page is 5 MB of script-drawn content, but did not view the rendering; the two SVG pictures I viewed as images, cropped to their upper 1400 pixels. How the first screen falls on a real viewport or a phone. The depth of the dualism Ren names: I can report which paired words read as good-and-bad to an outsider, not whether the concepts can be re-said without the pairs. Note also that the scratchpad I fetched the site into already held files from earlier sessions; I wrote only site/index.html, site/map.html, site/connections.html, t.svg, s.svg and their PNG previews there, and nothing in the repository.
